## Routes

- **The Founders' Walk** (2.5 km walking): Stanford Mausoleum → Angel of Grief → Arizona Cactus Garden → Cantor Arts Center → Rodin Sculpture Garden → The Oval → Main Quad → Memorial Church
- **Big Game Day** (2.1 km walking): White Plaza & The Claw → Old Union → Memorial Auditorium → Hoover Tower → Frost Amphitheater → Stanford Stadium
- **The 1906 Earthquake Walk** (2.4 km walking): Stanford Mausoleum → Angel of Grief → Cantor Arts Center → Memorial Court & The Burghers → Main Quad → Memorial Church → Green Library
- **The Farm & the Presidents** (3.3 km walking): Red Barn → Lake Lagunita → Papua New Guinea Sculpture Garden → The Knoll → Lou Henry Hoover House
- **One Piece of Land** (4.6 km walking): Red Barn → Lake Lagunita → Arizona Cactus Garden → Stanford Mausoleum → Angel of Grief → Main Quad

## v0.3 research notes (Oct 25, 2026, ~5 AM PT)

- **Six new landmarks:** Gates Computer Science, Lou Henry Hoover House, Papua New Guinea Sculpture Garden, Lake Lagunita, The Knoll and Memorial Court & The Burghers. Coordinates come from OSM Nominatim.
- **PNG garden residency length:** sources disagree. Stanford Report (2024) says four months, the Visitor Center says five and STANFORD magazine says three, so the card says "spent months."
- **Knoll start date dropped:** Palo Alto Stanford Heritage says construction began in 1913, the year Wilbur became president, but CCRMA says Wilbur was elected on Oct. 13, 1915, and PCAD dates construction to 1917–18. The card gives only the completion year, 1918, which all sources agree on. Hoover's "Portuguese Gothic" jab (PAST) was swapped for the "insane asylum" line, which STANFORD magazine sources.
- **Hoover House:** PCAD says Hoover deeded the house to Stanford after his own death (1964). NPS and Wikipedia's cited NPS source say he did it after Lou's death in 1944. The card follows NPS. The draftsman's name is "Davis" (California OHP), not "Davus" (NPS).
- **Lagunita:** Stanford 125's claims (built in 1878, 118 million gallons, bonfire ended in 1993 over tiger salamanders) were left out because 125.stanford.edu returns 403 and couldn't be re-verified. The card uses the Stanford Conservation Program (late 1870s, Chinese laborers, boating 1893–2000) and Stanford Report (Water Carnival, May 6, 1938 boathouse collapse, tiger salamander habitat). Its timeline sort year, 1878, is an approximation of "late 1870s."
- **Burghers:** no reliable source for the exact year the figures were installed in Memorial Court was found, so the card doesn't give one. The 1884 commission and 1346–47 siege come from the Musée Rodin. The 89-work February 1974 gift and "largest collection outside the Musée Rodin" come from STANFORD magazine.
- **Gates/Google:** the room 360 naming story comes from a Stanford-hosted page by Prof. David Koller (graphics.stanford.edu), which times out to curl but is indexed. "Moved off campus and incorporated in 1998" comes from NSF.
- **Link check (v0.3 additions):** all new URLs return 200 except sup.org (429 rate limit to scripts) and graphics.stanford.edu (timeout to scripts). Both are reachable through normal search and fetch.

## Corrections vs v0

- **Hoover Tower:** the marker moved about 40 m west to the tower itself (37.42762, -122.16699, OSM/Wikipedia).
- **Frost Amphitheater:** the marker moved about 120 m north to the bowl (37.43056, -122.16583, Wikipedia).
- **Encina Hall:** the marker moved about 60 m to the building center (OSM).
- **The Dish:** "finished in the 1960s" is now "built in 1961" (SRI/Wikipedia), and the marker moved about 40 m to the antenna. The vague claim of "hundreds of thousands of hikers a year" was replaced with the sourced 3.5-mile loop.
- **Memorial Church:** v0's "4,332 pipes" for the Fisk-Nanney organ was dropped because Stanford sources disagree: facts.stanford.edu says 4,332 and orsl.stanford.edu says 4,422. The card now says "five pipe organs" without a pipe count.
- **Green Library:** v0's "Lane Reading Room" claim was removed because it couldn't be verified.
- **Angel of Grief:** "the original fell in 1906" now gives the detail that the marble canopy collapsed onto the angel, and that the replacement went up in 1908 (Stanford quake06).
- **Encina / Hoover:** the claim that Hoover lived there is now framed as Jordan's "Room 38" story. The Stanford Historical Society calls it possibly apocryphal.
- **Frost:** v0's Church & Kiler credit was confirmed by Stanford Live (Wikipedia credits Kiler alone).
- **Stadium:** the build time is now "a matter of months" because sources disagree (GoStanford says about 4, Wikipedia says 5).

## v0.4: Cardinal book threads (verified Oct 25, 2026, ~8:30 AM PT)

Book-part mapping is a draft for Kyle to confirm. All thread facts were checked against the linked pages (all returned HTTP 200 on Oct 25). NPS pages differ on David Hewes's relationship to Stanford ("friend" vs "brother-in-law"), so the card leaves it out.

### 🚂 The Railroad Fortune (book: Ledger / Toll / Octopus (draft mapping))

Stops: Cantor Arts Center → Main Quad → Memorial Church → Stanford Mausoleum

- Leland Stanford was president of the Central Pacific Railroad, the western half of the first transcontinental line, and a former governor of California. [NPS: Golden Spike National Historic Site](https://www.nps.gov/articles/goldenspike.htm) [Stanford University: Our History](https://www.stanford.edu/about/history/)
- The Central Pacific recruited more than 11,000 workers from China. Stanford himself said that without them it would have been impossible to finish the western portion of the line. [NPS: Golden Spike National Historic Site](https://www.nps.gov/articles/goldenspike.htm)
- On May 10, 1869, at Promontory Summit, Utah, Stanford received the two golden spikes at the ceremony that joined the Central Pacific and Union Pacific tracks. [NPS: Golden Spike National Historic Site](https://www.nps.gov/articles/goldenspike.htm)
- The real Golden Spike is now in the Cantor Arts Center collection. David Hewes, who commissioned it, took it home after the ceremony and gave it to Stanford in 1892. [NPS Golden Spike NHP: FAQ](https://www.nps.gov/gosp/faqs.htm)
- After Leland died in 1893 the university faced severe money shortages, and Jane Stanford kept it going by selling many of her remaining assets, including a jewelry collection that fetched $500,000. [Stanford University: Our History](https://www.stanford.edu/about/history/)

### 🕊️ A Memorial to a Son (book: The Boy and the Farm (draft mapping))

Stops: Stanford Mausoleum → Angel of Grief → Arizona Cactus Garden → Main Quad → Memorial Church

- Leland Stanford Jr., the Stanfords' only child, died of typhoid fever in 1884 at age 15. His parents founded the university in 1885 as his memorial, resolving that “the children of California shall be our children.” [Stanford University: Our History](https://www.stanford.edu/about/history/)
- Its legal name is still Leland Stanford Junior University. It opened on October 1, 1891. [Stanford University: Our History](https://www.stanford.edu/about/history/)
- The Stanfords wanted it nonsectarian, coeducational and affordable, combining the liberal arts with training in science and engineering. [Stanford University: Our History](https://www.stanford.edu/about/history/)

### 🐎 The Farm (book: The Boy and the Farm (draft mapping))

Stops: Red Barn → Lake Lagunita → Arizona Cactus Garden → The Oval

- The university was built on the Stanford family's Palo Alto stock farm, an 8,180-acre property. [Stanford University: Our History](https://www.stanford.edu/about/history/)
- At the farm in 1878–79, Eadweard Muybridge's battery of cameras proved that a galloping horse lifts all four hooves off the ground (see the Red Barn card). [Stanford Red Barn: History](https://redbarn.stanford.edu/history)
- Farm laborers, many of them Chinese workers, dug Lagunita in the late 1870s as a reservoir for the farm (see the Lake Lagunita card). [Stanford Conservation Program: Lagunita](https://conservation.stanford.edu/education-outreach/lagunita-interpretation/interpretive-signs)
- The free Marguerite campus shuttle is named after a 19th-century horse that pulled a jitney between campus and Palo Alto. [Stanford University: Our History](https://www.stanford.edu/about/history/)

### 💻 Terman & the Valley (book: The Engineer's Century / Park (draft mapping))

Stops: The Dish → Gates Computer Science

- Engineering professor Frederick Terman, later dean and provost and dubbed the “Father of Silicon Valley,” encouraged students to develop and commercialize their ideas. [Stanford University: Our History](https://www.stanford.edu/about/history/)
- With Terman's encouragement, Stanford graduates Bill Hewlett and Dave Packard founded Hewlett-Packard on January 1, 1939. Their first product was the 200A audio oscillator. [HP History: 1930s timeline](https://www.hp.com/hpinfo/abouthp/histnfacts/timeline/hist_30s.html) [Stanford University: Our History](https://www.stanford.edu/about/history/)
- In 1951 Stanford opened what is now Stanford Research Park on its own land, the brainchild of Terman. Varian Associates became the first tenant. [Stanford University: Our History](https://www.stanford.edu/about/history/) [Stanford Research Park: About](https://stanfordresearchpark.com/about/)
- The Cold War gave rise to the Dish, and in 1998 Larry Page and Sergey Brin founded Google (see the Dish and Gates cards). [Stanford University: Our History](https://www.stanford.edu/about/history/) [NSF: On the Origins of Google](https://www.nsf.gov/impacts/google)

### 🏞️ One Piece of Land (book: The Octopus / The Boy and the Farm (draft mapping))

Stops: Red Barn → Lake Lagunita → Arizona Cactus Garden → Stanford Mausoleum → Angel of Grief → Main Quad

- In 1876 Leland Stanford bought Mayfield Grange (about 650 acres along San Francisquito Creek) and kept buying until he held over 8,000 acres. At its height the Palo Alto Stock Farm employed 150 workers and boarded 600 horses. The Victorian Red Barn, built 1878–1880, was its training stable. [Stanford Red Barn: History](https://redbarn.stanford.edu/history)
- In June 1878, a dozen cameras triggered by wires across the track photographed a Stanford trotter in sequence, showing a running horse fully aloft, a first step toward motion pictures. [STANFORD magazine: The Man Who Stopped Time](https://stanfordmag.org/contents/the-man-who-stopped-time) [Library of Congress: The Horse in Motion](https://www.loc.gov/resource/ppmsca.23778/)
- The farm closed in 1903; President Donald Tresidder reopened the barn for riding in 1946. [Stanford Red Barn: History](https://redbarn.stanford.edu/history)
- Lake Lagunita was built in 1878 as a stock pond and water reservoir for the Palo Alto Stock Farm and vineyard. [Stanford 125: Lagunita](https://125.stanford.edu/lagunita/) [Stanford Habitat Conservation Plan, ch. 3](https://hcp.stanford.edu/2013HCP/HCP%20March%202013/Stanford%20HCP%20Ch%203%20August%202013%20approved%20%28Rev%203%2023%202016%29.pdf)
- The earthen berm is 16 ft tall and 2,500 ft long, and the porous lakebed loses about 500 gallons a minute. [Stanford Habitat Conservation Plan, ch. 3](https://hcp.stanford.edu/2013HCP/HCP%20March%202013/Stanford%20HCP%20Ch%203%20August%202013%20approved%20%28Rev%203%2023%202016%29.pdf)
- When the university opened in 1891, Stanford let students row there. Boating ran until 2000, and the lake always dried out by summer. [Stanford 125: Lagunita](https://125.stanford.edu/lagunita/) [Stanford Conservation Program: historic maps and photos of Lagunita](https://conservation.stanford.edu/education-outreach/lagunita-interpretation/historic-maps-and-photos-lagunita)
- The Big Game bonfire on the lakebed ended in 1993 after it was found to be a breeding ground for the endangered California tiger salamander. [Stanford 125: Lagunita](https://125.stanford.edu/lagunita/)
- The Arizona Cactus Garden was designed for Jane and Leland Stanford by landscape gardener Rudolph Ulrich in the early 1880s, beside the site of a country mansion they planned. [Pacific Horticulture: Rudolph Ulrich's Arizona Gardens](https://pacifichorticulture.org/articles/rudolph-ulrichs-arizona-gardens/)
- Stanford sent Ulrich to the Sonoran Desert, where he collected specimens by horse-drawn wagon and shipped them back by rail. [Stanford Report, 2003](https://news.stanford.edu/stories/2003/01/sun-shines-century-old-cactus-garden)
- After Leland Jr. died in 1884 the mansion was abandoned; the garden and the Arboretum are the only remnants of that estate plan. [Pacific Horticulture: Rudolph Ulrich's Arizona Gardens](https://pacifichorticulture.org/articles/rudolph-ulrichs-arizona-gardens/)
- It was maintained until the 1920s, partly by two former Stanford family staff, Chung and Ah Wah, then largely neglected. [Stanford Report, 2003](https://news.stanford.edu/stories/2003/01/sun-shines-century-old-cactus-garden)
- Leland Stanford Jr. died of typhoid fever in Florence on March 13, 1884, at age 15. His parents turned their fortune into a university in his name and built this granite and marble tomb, completed in 1889 for more than $100,000. Leland Jr.'s casket was moved here on June 29, 1893, five days after his father's burial; Jane joined them after her death in 1905. [Stanford Founders' Celebration: Mausoleum area (PDF)](https://founders.stanford.edu/sites/g/files/sbiybj15291/files/media/file/mausoleumarea_final.pdf) [Stanford & the 1906 Earthquake: Entrance and Palm Drive](https://quake06.stanford.edu/entrance-and-palm-drive) [Stanford & the 1906 Earthquake: timeline](https://quake06.stanford.edu/timeline-events)
- This marble angel is a memorial to Henry Clay Lathrop, Jane Stanford's youngest brother. It copies The Angel of Grief, the sculpture William Wetmore Story made in 1894 for his wife's grave in Rome. Jane commissioned the first copy in 1901. [Stanford Founders' Celebration: Mausoleum area (PDF)](https://founders.stanford.edu/sites/g/files/sbiybj15291/files/media/file/mausoleumarea_final.pdf) [Stanford & the 1906 Earthquake: Entrance and Palm Drive](https://quake06.stanford.edu/entrance-and-palm-drive) [Wikipedia (secondary)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angel_of_Grief)
- Leland and Jane Stanford laid the cornerstone on May 14, 1887, the day their son Leland Jr. would have turned 19. When the university opened on October 1, 1891, the Inner Quad welcomed more than 500 students and 15 faculty. [Stanford & the 1906 Earthquake: timeline](https://quake06.stanford.edu/timeline-events) [Stanford Digital Repository: 1888 campus plan (Shepley, Rutan & Coolidge; F.L. & J.C. Olmsted)](https://purl.stanford.edu/wf779fg7366) [Wikipedia (secondary): Main Quad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Quad_(Stanford_University))
- Thirty palms were dug up from the garden and replanted in the Main Quad's circles when the university was built. [Pacific Horticulture: Rudolph Ulrich's Arizona Gardens](https://pacifichorticulture.org/articles/rudolph-ulrichs-arizona-gardens/)

## v0.4: Daily Hunt

Daily Hunt picks 3 landmarks per Pacific-time day from a fixed seed; clues are the existing sourced quiz questions. No new historical facts.
